name: Zero-Price Effect
description: Demand for a free item is disproportionately higher than its price-discount alone would predict — 'FREE!' exerts an extra pull on choice beyond what standard demand curves account for.
design_relevance_note: Explains why 'free shipping' or 'free trial' framing outperforms an equivalent-value discount in real conversion data.
myth_risk_note: Previously rated moderate on the narrow basis of a discovery pass finding only one additional candidate beyond the original source. Resolved to low: two genuine independent extensions now exist (multicomponent bundling generalization; a documented time-pressure boundary condition), and a fresh check confirmed no meta-analysis exists to promote this further -- the literature genuinely is thinner than more famous effects in this corpus, not a red flag, just a real characteristic of a comparatively newer (2007) effect.
prevalence_note: Widely cited in pricing and growth-marketing design discourse, though less universally taught than core Cialdini-adjacent principles.

findings.description: Comparing three candidate psychological mechanisms for the zero-price effect — social norms, difficulty of computing net benefit ('mapping difficulty'), and affect (a positive feeling toward getting something free) — affect emerged as the most likely explanation for why demand for free items exceeds what a standard cost-benefit analysis predicts.
findings.source_title: Zero as a Special Price: The True Value of Free Products

findings.description: In experiments holding the price gap between two goods constant, demand shifted dramatically toward the cheaper good specifically when its price was reduced to exactly zero (versus an equivalent low positive price): far more participants chose the free option and far fewer chose the costlier option than a standard cost-benefit (net-value) calculation would predict, indicating people treat a price of zero as conferring extra benefit, not merely as a cost reduction.
findings.source_title: Zero as a Special Price: The True Value of Free Products

applications.title: Amazon's France sales lagged under a 20-cent shipping charge and rose once shipping became fully free
applications.description: CXL's article on the persuasive power of 'free' repeats a widely-cited business anecdote (sourced to Chris Anderson's book 'Free') that when Amazon rolled out free shipping across multiple countries, sales rose everywhere except France, where a nominal 20-cent shipping charge remained instead of zero; once that charge was dropped to literal zero, French sales rose too -- illustrating that a price near zero behaves very differently from a price of exactly zero, the core signature of the zero-price effect, rather than a smooth, proportional response to a small discount.
applications.ethical_note: Free shipping is a genuine value transfer to the customer (no cost is hidden or shifted elsewhere in this account), not a manipulative pricing dark pattern.

applications.title: Skincare brand NuFace raised average order value by adding a free-shipping spending threshold
applications.description: CXL's article on the persuasive power of 'free' cites a VWO-published case study in which skincare brand NuFace increased average order value (AOV) by 7.32% after introducing a minimum-spend threshold that unlocked free shipping -- a common ecommerce mechanism that leverages the zero-price effect by making the jump from 'costs something' to 'costs literally nothing' the reward for buying slightly more.
applications.ethical_note: A transparent, opt-in spending threshold that customers can see and choose to meet for a real benefit, not a hidden or coercive pricing mechanism.
